claims.text: The system consists of sub-10 nm equiatomic Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles.
The as-synthesized nanoparticles are a single-phase solid solution with high configurational entropy.
A vacuum atmosphere prevents oxidation during heating.
Heating from 300 K to 1000 K triggers rapid phase separation in the nanoparticles.
Surface-energy-driven segregation overrides the hypothesized sluggish-diffusion stabilization.
Au and Cu are the low-surface-energy elements in this alloy.
Au and Cu segregate to particle surfaces while Co, Ni, and Pt form compositionally enriched cores.
Elevated temperature enhances diffusion sufficiently to enable rapid structural evolution.
The high surface-to-volume ratio of sub-10 nm particles makes surface diffusion pathways dominant.
Configurational entropy is insufficient to counteract surface-energy penalties and the driving force for phase separation at this particle size.
Chemical-potential gradients between differently sized particles cause smaller particles to dissolve and material to redeposit on larger particles by Ostwald ripening.
Ostwald ripening causes the disappearance of the smallest particles.
Surface-energy minimization changes particle morphology from spherical to faceted or irregular shapes.
Under the sluggish-diffusion baseline, the particles would retain a single phase with minimal size and shape change up to 1000 K.
Sluggish diffusion is typically observed in bulk high-entropy alloys.
The sluggish-diffusion assumption holds for particles larger than 50 nm or for bulk alloys.
The sluggish-diffusion assumption breaks down for sub-10 nm particles because surface effects dominate.
The proposed surface-driven behavior should become observable within minutes above 600 K.
In-situ high-temperature TEM combined with EDS or EELS can discriminate retention of a single phase from ripening and elemental surface segregation.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome correctly describes dissolution of the smallest particles and redeposition onto larger particles, whereas the experiment describes the signature broadly as 'rapid particle size reduction.' Ostwald ripening normally decreases the smallest-particle population while increasing the characteristic or average size of the surviving particles, so the stated measurement direction is ambiguous and potentially opposite to the predicted population-level outcome.
